title: How particles move in solids, liquids and gases
examples: How are particles arranged in a solid?
Why can you pour a liquid?
Why does a gas fill a room?

figure.name: x-particles
figure.label: Ice cube: a solid
figure.ask: Why does a solid keep its shape?

explain.say: Imagine you could shrink smaller than a speck of dust and stand on an ice cube. Look at the board. You would see tiny particles packed tight in neat rows. They only jiggle on the spot. That is why a solid keeps its shape.

draw.name: x-particles
draw.label: Ice cube: a solid
draw.ask: Why does a solid keep its shape?

explain.say: Now let me show you the real thing in 3D: solid, liquid and gas. Look at the solid, the liquid and the gas. Tap any part, and I will tell you what it does.

draw.text: How particles move in solids, liquids and gases

explain.say: Now look at liquid water. See how the particles still touch, but slide past each other? That is why you can pour a liquid, and why it takes the shape of its cup. Can you think of a liquid you pour every day?

draw.name: x-particles
draw.label: Water: a liquid
draw.ask: Why can you pour a liquid?

explain.say: Here is a gas, like steam from your kettle. Watch the particles zoom about, far apart. They spread out to fill any space. Which moves the most so far: the solid, the liquid or the gas?

draw.name: x-particles
draw.label: Steam: a gas
draw.ask: Why does a gas spread out?

explain.say: Look what happens when you warm ice. The particles get more energy, which means more power to move. They jiggle harder and break out of their rows, so the solid melts into a liquid. Do you think cooling does the opposite?

draw.name: x-particles
draw.label: Ice melting
draw.ask: What happens to particles when something melts?

explain.say: Great work! Now sort things from your home. Ice and a coin are solids, milk and honey are liquids, steam and the air in a balloon are gases. Wow: the same water particles can be all three. Only their energy changes.

faq.q: Why does a solid keep its shape?
faq.a: In a solid the particles are held tightly in fixed places. They can only vibrate on the spot, so the shape stays the same.
asks: Why can't you pour a solid?

faq.q: Why can you pour a liquid?
faq.a: The particles in a liquid stay close together but can slide past each other. So a liquid flows and takes the shape of its container.
asks: Why does water take the shape of a glass?

faq.q: Why does a gas spread out?
faq.a: Gas particles move fast in all directions with big gaps between them. They keep moving until they fill the whole space.
asks: Why does a gas fill a room?

faq.q: What happens to particles when something melts?
faq.a: Heating gives the particles more energy. They vibrate harder until they break free of their fixed places, and the solid becomes a liquid.
asks: What is melting in the particle model?

faq.a: Yes. Gas particles have big gaps between them, so you can push them closer, like air in a bicycle pump. Solids and liquids hardly squash at all.

facts: Particles in a solid vibrate about fixed positions; in a liquid they slide past each other; in a gas they move fast and randomly with large gaps.
Steam at 100 °C takes up roughly 1,600 times more space than the same mass of liquid water.
